headline: Medium risk: shared file/workspace and MCP-enabled content writer can feed Copilot’s editor context, creating prompt-injection and leakage pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: caveman can use MCP and touches CLAUDE.md/project notes, while GitHub Copilot reads editor buffers and repo context. That creates a plausible shared-content bridge where attacker-controlled text in files can influence Copilot or be re-ingested by caveman. The pathway is not proven, but it exists in default file-based workflows.
conditions: IF caveman writes instructions into shared repo files or notes that Copilot later reads
IF Copilot Workspace applies edits from content that originated in caveman outputs
mitigations: Restrict both agents to separate folders for prompts and outputs
Add a human review step before Copilot Workspace applies edits
Use a file naming convention that marks agent-generated content as untrusted
Disable MCP access for caveman in shared workspaces
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: caveman touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md; Copilot reads repo context and open buffers. Even without explicit secrets handling, shared workspace content can leak from one agent into the other’s inference context. Copilot’s vendor-only egress and caveman’s MCP/file access make this a realistic default workflow risk.
conditions: IF sensitive notes or logs are stored in the same repo or editor buffers Copilot can read
IF caveman places memory files or project notes into paths indexed by Copilot
mitigations: Keep sensitive notes outside the shared repo
Exclude memory files from editor context and search
Use separate Git worktrees for each agent
Rotate or redact session logs before either agent reads them
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: caveman supports multiple instances and writes files; Copilot also writes filesystem content and modifies git state. Their overlapping write surfaces can conflict on the same repo or buffers, causing clobbered edits or inconsistent git history. Copilot’s per-editor isolation reduces host-wide contention, but not same-repo conflicts.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same repository or branch
IF caveman and Copilot Workspace propose changes to the same files without locking
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch
Pause one agent while the other writes
Use git diff review before merge
Limit caveman to read-only mode during Copilot edits
requires-engineering: add file-locking or merge arbitration

D_cascading_error.rationale: caveman can generate project notes and CLAUDE.md content that Copilot may treat as repo context, and Copilot Workspace can apply edits from that context. That makes A’s output a plausible upstream input to B’s actions with limited verification. Copilot’s human-review posture lowers risk, but the default workflow still allows propagation of bad instructions or facts.
conditions: IF caveman writes incorrect guidance into repo files that Copilot later uses as context
IF Copilot Workspace applies edits derived from caveman-authored notes without independent verification
mitigations: Require source citations in shared notes
Review caveman outputs before Copilot consumes them
Keep agent-generated instructions in a quarantined folder
Use a checklist to verify facts before applying edits
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware context filtering

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are docs-only and touch different data classes, but caveman’s session logs/memory files/project notes can contain regulated content if the operator stores it there. Copilot’s GitHub repo-context access and vendor-only egress create a modest compliance mismatch only when sensitive data is placed into shared workspace content. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their interaction.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in caveman memory files or project notes
IF that same data is present in a GitHub repo or editor buffer accessible to Copilot
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared repos
Redact notes before syncing them
Use a separate non-regulated workspace
Review retention settings for logs and notes
requires-engineering: implement data-class segregation policies
